title: What If One Fish Took Over a River? In Illinois, It's 75% of the Catch

scenes.text: What if one fish took over a river? In parts of Illinois, it already has.
Asian carp were imported to eat weeds and algae in catfish ponds. Nobody thought they could breed here.
Floods in the early 1970s set thousands loose. In one stretch of the Illinois River they're now over 75 percent of all fish by weight.
Silver carp panic at boat motors and launch into the air: 25-pound fish that have broken boaters' arms and jaws.
Chicago's canal leads to Lake Michigan. An electric barrier guards it. In a test, one tagged fish got through, hitchhiking between barges.
So the US is building a 1.2 billion dollar fish fortress: bubble curtains, underwater speakers, a lock that flushes fish back. And a new menu name: copi.

description:
What if a single fish took over America's rivers? Invasive carp, imported in the 1960s and 70s to clean weeds and algae from catfish ponds, escaped in floods in the early 1970s and now make up more than 75 percent of the fish biomass in one section of the Illinois River.
Silver carp leap from the water when startled by boats, and 25-pound fish have broken boaters' arms and jaws. To keep them out of Lake Michigan, an electric barrier near Romeoville guards the Chicago canal; in one test only one of 130 tagged carp got past, apparently carried between barges. The Brandon Road Lock and Dam project, now estimated at about 1.2 billion dollars, adds bubble curtains, acoustic deterrents and a flushing lock. Illinois has rebranded the fish as copi to encourage people to eat it.
